title: Our Mutual Friend: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: Opening: The Will and the Body—Who Is John Harmon?

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, a close reading of Charles Dickens's great, strange, final completed novel.
Over the course of this series, we'll be moving through the novel passage by passage, bringing together three remarkable readers to argue, illuminate, and occasionally disagree.
Today we begin at one of the most audacious moments in nineteenth-century fiction: the chapter in which a man we have been told is dead explains, to himself and to us, precisely how he came to be so.
The question of who John Harmon really is — and what it costs him to keep that secret — sits at the very heart of this novel.
Let me introduce our three guests.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don and one of the great traditionalist voices in English literary criticism.

He reads novels as moral fables — stories about character under pressure — and he will keep us honest about what Dickens is actually doing with his people, as opposed to what we might wish he were doing.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who has spent a career understanding the institutions that Victorian fiction depicts.
When the novel turns on questions of wills, identities, and the machinery of the law, James is exactly the person you want in the room.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic and passionate re-reader of Victorian fiction who first encountered this novel as a teenager and has never quite recovered.
She brings us the experience of reading — what is thrilling, what is funny, what is genuinely strange about these pages.
Edmund, I want to start with you, because you've always been drawn to Dickens's treatment of inherited wealth and corrupted children.
In Chapter Thirty, we finally get John Harmon's own account of himself.
What does Dickens give us in that extraordinary passage about the origins of the deception?
One is grateful, as always, for a text that does the work of explaining itself — though Dickens, typically, takes his time arriving at the explanation.
What strikes me most forcefully about this passage is its understanding of moral drift.
John Harmon does not choose villainy.
He lapses into his condition — and Dickens is precise about this —
"as many a man lapses into many a condition, without perceiving the accumulative power of its separate circumstances."
That word 'accumulative' is doing enormous work.
It is not a single fall; it is a series of small concessions, each one making the next seem reasonable.
This is very much a conservative moral psychology, I would suggest — an understanding that the self is not mastered by grand gestures of virtue, but imperilled by gradual, barely-noticed yielding.
And behind it all, of course, is the father's money — that corrosive inheritance which Dickens identifies, quite brilliantly, as the root cause.

The deception was conceived, Dickens tells us, in "the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil — never yet for good within his knowledge then — of his father and his father's wealth on all within their influence."
That parenthetical — 'never yet for good within his knowledge then' — is among the most quietly devastating things in the novel.
James, you've spent time with the legal architecture of the Victorian inheritance system.
Does Harmon's predicament make sense in real institutional terms — this idea of being legally dead while biologically alive?
It makes a great deal of sense, and what's remarkable is how carefully Dickens has thought through the legal consequences, even if he doesn't parade them.
A man presumed dead by the police, plastered across London walls as 'wanted' under the name Julius Handford, effectively has no legal identity at all.
He cannot inherit, cannot testify, cannot contract.
Dickens captures this with that marvellous triple identity — the oakum-headed sailor, Rokesmith the secretary, Julius Handford the wanted man — all being, as the text says,
"as like that same lost wanted Mr Julius Handford, as never man was like another in this world."

That repetition — 'as never man was like another in this world' — applied first to the sailor becoming Handford, then immediately to Rokesmith also becoming Handford — is Dickens showing us the legal trap through the form of the sentence itself.
They are all the same man, and yet none of them can legally be that man.
There is something genuinely chilling about the institutional thoroughness of his erasure — and Dickens understood that perfectly.
What gets me every time I return to these chapters is the physical sensation of Harmon's narration.
It isn't an account of remembered events — it's an account of the dissolution of a self.
Listen to this passage describing the attack and the aftermath — it reads almost like a fever dream:
"I saw a figure like myself lying dressed in my clothes on a bed.
What might have been, for anything I knew, a silence of days, weeks, months, years, was broken by a violent wrestling of men all over the room."
That list — days, weeks, months, years — suspended in the middle of a sentence — is extraordinary.
Time itself has gone missing along with the identity.
And then Harmon can't even name himself — 'I could not have said that my name was John Harmon — I could not have thought it — I didn't know it.'
The self has genuinely come untethered — and it will take an act of almost pure will to bring it back.
And that act of will is extraordinary in itself.
Edmund, Caroline has pointed us toward the drowning passage — this moment of consciousness returning in the water.
It reads almost like a secular baptism, wouldn't you say?
I would say more than 'almost.'
There is something deeply — one might almost say liturgically — formal about this moment of self-reclamation.
Harmon calls his own name three times, like a priest calling a soul back to the body:
"This is John Harmon drowning! John Harmon, struggle for your life. John Harmon, call on Heaven and save yourself!"
The triple invocation is not accidental — Dickens knows precisely what he is doing with the Christian resonance.
But I want to insist on something further: that 'call on Heaven' is not mere rhetorical decoration.
It locates the recovery of selfhood in a moral — indeed, a theological — act of will, not merely a biological instinct for survival.
The man who resurfaces is a different man from the one who went under — and Dickens earns that transformation.
I don't want to puncture Edmund's theological reading, because it's a good one — but I'd add the social dimension.
What Harmon resurfaces into is not merely life — it's a particular kind of social death-in-life.
He himself describes looking into a churchyard and feeling, as he puts it,
"that I no more hold a place among the living than these dead do, and even to know that I lie buried somewhere else, as they lie buried here."
That is not a metaphor for spiritual alienation — or not only that.
It is a description of a man who has no legal standing, no social position, no name he can use in public.
The Victorian self was, in ways we've largely forgotten, a juridical construction.
Without papers, without a recognized name, without a will that names you — you simply don't exist.
And then there's the resolution Rokesmith arrives at — which I find almost unbearably poignant.
Having spent the night, as Dickens puts it, on the 'sexton-task of piling earth above John Harmon,' he wakes resolved to remain a ghost.
The novel gives it to us with the most extraordinary delicacy:

"No ghost should trouble Mr and Mrs Boffin's peace; invisible and voiceless, the ghost should look on for a little while longer at the state of existence out of which it had departed, and then should for ever cease to haunt the scenes in which it had no place."
'For ever cease to haunt the scenes in which it had no place' — that is the saddest line.
He is not planning to live — he is planning to disappear, quietly, so that the people he loves will not be disturbed by his existence.
That is the strange moral beauty at the centre of this whole plot.
Which brings us, before we close this opening segment, to the question of what Dickens himself says about the design behind all of this — because he is unusually forthcoming on the subject.
Edmund, you've written about the postscript passages in which Dickens addresses his readers directly.
What do we make of an author who tells us, in effect, that we were right to suspect what we suspected all along?
It is an act of extraordinary authorial confidence — which, in lesser hands, would be insufferable.
Dickens says, quite plainly, that he foresaw the misreading and was not alarmed by it.
The precise formulation is worth hearing:

"I foresaw the likelihood that a class of readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John Harmon was not slain, and that Mr John Rokesmith was he."
'A class of readers and commentators' — that is a withering designation, delivered with perfect courtesy.
He is asking his audience to extend him the patience due to an artist who knows what he is doing — and simultaneously reminding them that very many readers failed to do so.
One recognises the tone, I confess, from certain faculty meetings.
What strikes me in the companion passage is the practical challenge he's describing — maintaining a secret subplot across nineteen monthly instalments.
Dickens puts it precisely — and it's worth sitting with:

"To keep for a long time unsuspected, yet always working itself out, another purpose originating in that leading incident, and turning it to a pleasant and useful account at last, was at once the most interesting and the most difficult part of my design."
'Always working itself out' — that phrase is the key to understanding why the Harmon plot never feels like mere contrivance.
The secret is not dormant — it is active in every scene, even when it's invisible to the reader.
That is a remarkable feat of structural engineering, and historians of serialization rather underestimate it.
There's something almost moving about Dickens's relationship with his readers in those postscript passages — the novelist who invented the mass audience, asking that audience to trust him.
We'll be returning to questions of design and disguise throughout this series.
But in the next segment, we turn from the question of who John Harmon is to the question of what he stands to inherit — the dust mounds, the money, and the world old Harmon made.

segments.title: A Young Woman's Appetite: Bella Before and After

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We've spent time this series on money, on dust, on the river — but today we turn to one of the novel's most quietly remarkable achievements: Bella Wilfer.
Bella begins the novel as a young woman who is frankly, unapologetically mercenary — and yet she becomes, through the course of it, something entirely different.
To explore that arc, I have three voices I trust enormously.
Sir Edmund Leigh brings his conviction that fiction is ultimately about individual moral character — tested, found wanting, or redeemed.
Professor James Blackstone sets the social and legal ground beneath Bella's feet — what it actually meant for a young woman of her class to choose poverty over prosperity.
And Caroline Woodcourt, who has lived with this novel since she was a girl, and who I suspect has re-read Bella's bedroom scenes more than once.
Let's begin at the opening of chapter thirty-eight, where Dickens poses the question directly.
The opening of that chapter is a genuine masterpiece of narrative teasing.
Dickens holds the ambiguity before us like a lens he refuses to focus.
He asks, in so many words: is Bella's perception faulty, or is Boffin genuinely corrupting?
And he does so with a phrase that is almost biblical in its weight.
'Was the Golden Dustman passing through the furnace of proof and coming out dross?'
The furnace of proof — that is the language of the Psalms, of the assay-house.
Gold is tested in fire, and either confirmed or found to be base metal.
What I find extraordinary is that this question, posed so early, is never quite resolved for us as readers — not immediately.
We must watch, as Bella watches, and trust our own moral perception.
And the thing is, Bella is watching with eyes that are very far from innocent.
She arrives at this moment of moral crisis already compromised — already someone who has told herself that money matters above most things.
And what I love about the bedroom scene in passage fifty-five is that Dickens lets her convict herself, in her own inner voice, and then immediately find herself contemptible for the conviction.
She sits in front of her looking-glass — Dickens keeps returning to that glass — and she has this wonderful, ferocious self-interrogation.
'What he said was very sensible, I am sure, and very true, I am sure. It is only what I often say to myself.'
And then, immediately, the pivot — almost before the sentence is finished.
'Don't I like it then? No, I don't like it, and, though he is my liberal benefactor, I disparage him for it.'
And then that extraordinary, scalding sign-off: 'what do you mean by this, you inconsistent little Beast?'
It's funny, yes — but it's also genuinely unsparing.
What strikes me, picking up from Caroline, is that the scene's comedy doesn't soften the social bite — it sharpens it.
A young woman of Bella's class in the 1860s had almost no legitimate path to financial security except through marriage.
Her mercenary values are not simply personal vanity — they are a rational response to a legal and economic structure that offered her almost nothing else.
So when Bella calls herself a 'Beast' for clinging to those values, she is, in a sense, condemning herself for seeing clearly.
The tragedy and the comedy are inseparable.
James raises a point I don't entirely disagree with, though I'd put it differently.
The conditions may explain the temptation — but they do not explain away the moral choice.
That is precisely what Dickens is interested in: not the sociology, but the soul.
And what he shows us, quite movingly, is that when Bella goes to bed that night, something has already shifted.
'A weariness upon her spirit which was more than the weariness of want of sleep.'
That is spiritual distress — recognised and named — which is something quite different from mere discomfort.
She is waking to herself, and the waking is painful.
And that waking continues — and accelerates — when she meets Lizzie Hexam.
There's a scene I find almost unbearably tender, where Bella is so confronted by the selflessness of Lizzie's love that she literally punishes herself for her own meanness.
She gives herself 'a penitential poke in the side' — which is funny, yes, but also absolutely specific to who Bella is.
She can't do grand gestures — so she does a small, private, bodily one.
The whole passage is set up by her own self-accusation — she hears herself thinking mercenary thoughts and the narrator gives her that magnificent line.
'There, you little mercenary wretch! Do you hear that? Ain't you ashamed of your self?'
That's Bella's conscience speaking — and Dickens pitches it perfectly between self-mockery and genuine shame.
And Lizzie Hexam is the catalyst she has no vocabulary for.
The passage in chapter forty-two makes this quite explicit — and quite moving.
Bella encounters Lizzie's unselfish passion and Dickens tells us, without any irony at all, that she had never experienced anything like it.
'She had never experienced anything like it, or thought of the existence of anything like it.'
That phrase — 'thought of the existence of anything like it' — is quite precise.
It is not merely that she has not felt such love — she has not conceived of it as a human possibility.
That is the measure of how enclosed her world has been.
Which makes the resolution, when it comes, all the more striking — because Bella's final choice is not romantic naivety.
She has seen, close up, what wealth does to a man she admired — she has watched Boffin change — and she refuses to be purchased.
Her father — dear, absurd R. Wilfer — summarises it for us, with that touching formality he brings to everything serious.

'This mercenary young person distantly related to myself felt that she must not sell her sense of what was right and what was wrong, and what was true and what was false, and what was just and what was unjust, for any price that could be paid to her by any one alive.'
The repetition of those paired opposites — right and wrong, true and false, just and unjust — reads almost like a legal formulation.
Which is fitting — because what Bella is refusing is, in effect, a contract.
A contract in which she exchanges her moral self for material comfort.
And R. Wilfer's phrasing — 'a mercenary young person distantly related to myself' — is one of Dickens's great comic gestures of love.
He speaks of his own daughter with this formal remove because he cannot quite bear the directness of his pride in her.
And it echoes back to that early label — Bella always called herself mercenary, a little proudly, a little defiantly.
Now the word is used to describe what she has overcome — and Wilfer uses it tenderly, with full irony.
The whole arc of Bella is in that single word, used twice in completely different moral registers.
That is a beautiful place to hold for a moment — the word 'mercenary,' reclaimed and transformed.
Edmund, James, Caroline — thank you.

In our next segment we move outward from Bella's private moral drama to the world that shaped it — the Boffin household, the golden dust, and what Dickens makes of the corrupting power of inheritance.

segments.title: The Comic Grotesque: Reading Dickens Aloud

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We've been exploring the novel's great themes — dust, money, identity, the river.
But today we turn to something equally essential: Dickens as a comic writer.
Not merely amusing — grotesquely, precisely, irresistibly funny.
With me today are Sir Edmund Leigh, the retired Oxford don who reads Dickens as a moralist above all — and suspects fashionable interpretations.
Professor James Blackstone, legal and social historian, who can tell us exactly what a Dust Contractor was and why it matters.
And Caroline Woodcourt, book critic and devoted re-reader of this novel, who has very strong opinions about which passages deserve to be read aloud.
Let's begin with what I think is the most quoted sentence in the entire novel.
Betty Higden, describing her ward Sloppy and his gift for reading newspapers.
'He do the Police in different voices.'
Caroline — that sentence has launched a thousand essays. What does it do to you as a reader?
Every single time, it stops me cold.
It's grammatically 'wrong,' of course — Betty Higden isn't a grammarian.
But that wrongness is the rightness of it.
Dickens is rendering a voice — not transcribing dialect as a curiosity, but giving us the full warmth and dignity of how Betty speaks.
And the tenderness of what she's saying — that this boy, this orphan nobody, is a beautiful reader.
The full sentence is worth hearing in context.
'You mightn't think it, but Sloppy is a beautiful reader of a newspaper. He do the Police in different voices.'
That 'you mightn't think it' — she knows exactly what the world thinks of Sloppy, and she's pushing back.
Caroline is quite right about the dignity — and I think that's the key that unlocks the comedy in this novel.
Dickens is not laughing at Betty Higden.
He is laughing with her — and more precisely, he is delighted by her.
There's a difference between the satirical grotesque — which Dickens deploys elsewhere with quite devastating effect — and this kind of tender comic portrait.
When we encounter the dust mountains in Book One, we are very much in the satirical register.
Mortimer's account of old Harmon's estate is almost a catalogue of mockery.
'Coal-dust, vegetable-dust, bone-dust, crockery dust, rough dust and sifted dust, — all manner of Dust.'
The repetition is relentless — and intentionally so. That final 'Dust' with a capital D is the novel's central joke and central indictment delivered simultaneously.
I want to stay with those dust heaps for a moment, because the comedy there has real teeth.
Dust contractors in mid-Victorian London were genuinely wealthy men.
The heaps contained everything the city discarded — ash, bone, rags, broken crockery — and it could all be sold and reprocessed.
When Dickens writes that the elder Harmon 'grew rich as a Dust Contractor, and lived in a hollow in a hilly country entirely composed of Dust,' that's not mere caricature.
'He grew rich as a Dust Contractor, and lived in a hollow in a hilly country entirely composed of Dust.'
That's accurate social geography. Men like that did surround themselves with their own accumulation.
The comedy is funny precisely because it's true. Dickens understood that the most grotesque things in Victorian life were not inventions.
And then there's the Wegg and Boffin reading scenes, which are in a completely different comic register again.
This is farce — glorious, precise, literary farce.
Wegg reading Gibbon to Boffin is one of the great set-pieces of the novel, and it works entirely on the gap between what the words say and what anyone present understands.
The passage describing Wegg's performance is a masterpiece of controlled bathos.

'Mr Wegg, in a dry unflinching way, entered on his task; going straight across country at everything that came before him; taking all the hard words, biographical and geographical; getting rather shaken by Hadrian, Trajan, and the Antonines; stumbling at Polybius.'
'Stumbling at Polybius' — pronounced Polly Beeious, Dickens tells us, supposed by Mr Boffin to be a Roman virgin.
I defy anyone to read that aloud without laughing.
What strikes me about that passage is the horsemanship metaphor running through it — 'going straight across country,' 'stumbling,' 'heavily unseated,' 'up again and galloping.'
Wegg is a literary steeplechase jockey, and Gibbon's Latin names are the fences.
But the comedy deepens when we follow Boffin out of the door afterwards.
Boffin standing in the moonlight, staggered by Roman history, is one of my favourite moments in all of Dickens.
He recounts the enormities as though reporting a disaster to himself.

'Commodious fights in that wild-beast-show, seven hundred and thirty-five times, in one character only! As if that wasn't stunning enough, a hundred lions is turned into the same wild-beast-show all at once!'
And then the self-reproach: 'I didn't think this morning there was half so many Scarers in Print. But I'm in for it now.'
'Scarers in Print.' That is a genuinely great comic coinage.
Boffin also calls Commodus 'Commodious' — which is not only mishearing but actually rather apt for a man of excessive appetites.
And 'Vittle-us' for Vitellius — Vitellius being notorious precisely for gluttony.
Boffin mispronounces the name in a way that accidentally captures the man's character. Dickens is very nearly making a classical joke here.
There's a whole other dimension of Dickensian comedy I want to raise — the manipulation comedy of the Lammles.
The opera-box scene where they conduct an entire romantic courtship on behalf of Fledgeby and Georgiana Podsnap, without either young person actually speaking to the other.
Dickens describes it with forensic detachment, and then delivers the punchline with perfect timing.

'Through this device the two young people conversed at great length and committed themselves to a variety of delicate sentiments, without having once opened their lips, save to say yes or no, and even that not to one another.'
The social machinery of courtship rendered as pure absurdist theatre. It's Wodehouse before Wodehouse.
And there's a cruelty underneath it, of course — Georgiana is being manipulated towards a marriage she doesn't understand.
The comedy doesn't dissolve the menace. They coexist, which is what makes Dickens so unsettling.
I'm reminded of the passage describing Bella Wilfer's character — which is also simultaneously charming and a little troubling.
The narrator describes her as having a quality both irresistible and unmoored.
'The wayward, playful, affectionate nature, giddy for want of the weight of some sustaining purpose, and capricious because it was always fluttering among little things.'
'Giddy for want of the weight of some sustaining purpose' — that's not a comic line, exactly, but it has the same quality of perfect precision.
And what saves her, in that scene with Lizzie, is simply being seen — and asking, with genuine uncertainty, 'Do you think you could, Lizzie?'
That is precisely the point at which Dickens's comedy shades into something closer to character study.
And I think the passage about Boffin and the 'Scarers' does the same thing, from the other direction.
Boffin is comic, yes — but he is also genuinely committed to educating himself, even when it causes him distress.
'I'm in for it now' is funny, but it is also a statement of moral resolution from a man who owns dust heaps and reads Gibbon in the evenings.
The comedy, when Dickens is at his best, is the character. They are not separate things.
That feels like the right note on which to pause — comedy and character as inseparable in Dickens's method.
From Sloppy doing the police in different voices, to Boffin reeling in the moonlight from the scarers in print — each comic moment is also a portrait.
We'll be back shortly to look at the novel's darker comedy — what happens when the jokes are on people who cannot afford to be the joke.

segments.title: Dust and Ashes: Boffin's Moral Test and the Machinery of Wealth

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's last completed novel apart, passage by passage, to see what's still beating at its heart.
I'm your host, and today we're inside one of the novel's most audacious conceits: the dust-heap as moral theatre.
What does it mean that the greatest fortune in the story is built on ash and refuse?
And what on earth is Dickens doing when he appears to corrupt the most beloved character in the book — the Golden Dustman himself?
To work through all of that, I'm joined by three exceptional readers of this novel.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who reads Dickens as a moralist above all — a writer testing individual character against the temptations of circumstance.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who will keep us honest about the real-world institutions Dickens is anatomising.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel for decades and cares passionately about what it feels like to read it.
Let's begin with the world the Boffins step into the moment their fortune is confirmed — a world of creatures.
The passage that opens this whole strand of the novel is almost gleefully vicious.
Dickens sets the scene in the blooming summer days — and that word 'blooming' is doing mischief already.
It sounds like abundance, like health — but what blooms in this novel is appetite.
Then comes the list, and this is where Dickens is almost having too much fun.
He writes — and I want to read this properly —
"behold all manner of crawling, creeping, fluttering, and buzzing creatures, attracted by the gold dust of the Golden Dustman!"
Crawling, creeping, fluttering, buzzing — four different modes of undignified locomotion assigned to the social climbers of England.
It is insect comedy, but the laughter has an edge to it.
Caroline is quite right that the comedy has an edge, but I would press a little further on what that edge is cutting.
Dickens is not, I think, primarily attacking a class of people in that passage.
He is attacking a condition of the soul — the condition of being drawn irresistibly toward another man's wealth without any corresponding attraction to the man.
That is what the insect imagery captures: creatures that navigate entirely by scent, by the smell of gold.
They have forfeited the faculty of moral judgment.
Which sets up, rather beautifully I think, the question the novel then asks about Boffin himself.
Can a good man retain his moral faculty when he is made the centre of that gravitational pull — when the gold dust is his own?
Before we follow Boffin's interior journey, I want to hold briefly on the exterior world Dickens is describing, because it was quite precisely real.
The dust-yards of Victorian London were genuine industrial enterprises — enormous mounds of household ash, cinders, and refuse, sorted by hand for anything of value.
Old Harmon had made a fortune from what other people threw away and wanted forgotten.
Dickens understood that perfectly when he wrote the passage about the heap of ashes that makes my blood move a little faster every time I encounter it.
He addresses Parliament directly, which even for Dickens is a bold rhetorical move:
"My lords and gentlemen and honourable boards, when you in the course of your dust-shovelling and cinder-raking have piled up a mountain of pretentious failure,
you must off with your honourable coats for the removal of it, and fall to the work with the power of all the queen's horses and all the queen's men, or it will come rushing down and bury us alive."
'Bury us alive.' That is not satirical distance — that is a genuine warning about social collapse.
The dust is not just wealth — it is the accumulated consequence of institutional negligence.
And it's against that mountain of consequence that Dickens places one man — Boffin — and asks whether goodness can survive it.
There's a passage describing Boffin's daily rhythm under the weight of his new wealth that I find almost unbearably precise.
That passage is one of the most quietly devastating things Dickens ever wrote, I think.
He describes Boffin at breakfast — unclouded, still recognisably himself — and then shows us the change setting in like weather.
The sentence that stops me every time is this one:
"It was as the day went on that the clouds gathered, and the brightness of the morning became obscured."
There's a grief in that sentence that the comedy keeps trying to suppress.
And then it becomes even more exact: the shadows of avarice lengthening as his own shadow lengthens, the night closing gradually around him.
He is becoming his own dust-heap — a man composting himself.
Caroline's phrase is arresting, though I should note that Dickens will not allow Boffin to compost entirely — and that is crucial to what the novel is actually doing.
There is an earlier passage about the Boffins that I would call the moral bedrock of the whole novel.
Dickens observes that these two — ignorant and unpolished as he carefully calls them — had guided themselves by a religious sense of duty.
And even the hardened nature of old Harmon, he says, could not entirely resist their moral straightness.
Then comes the aphorism — and Dickens earns it fully:
"For, Evil often stops short at itself and dies with the doer of it; but Good, never."
It is a Johnsonian sentence — the kind of moral statement that doesn't argue, it asserts, because the observation is too deep for argument.
Boffin's goodness is unkillable — that is the premise on which the whole subsequent drama rests.
Edmund's reading is persuasive as a moral account, but I want to add the institutional dimension that I think Dickens is also pressing.
When Boffin cries out in his darkest moment — and it is a genuinely dark moment — the specific horror he names is the workhouse.
The text reads:
"'Dreadful, dreadful, dreadful! I shall die in a workhouse!' cried the Golden Dustman, with his hands to his head."
Now for a Victorian reader, the workhouse was not an abstraction — it was the ultimate institutional humiliation, the place you went when society had finished with you.
The miser's deepest fear is not poverty as suffering — it is poverty as public disgrace, as institutional disposal.
Boffin's cry is funny on the surface, but it points directly at the machinery Dickens indicts in that address to Parliament.
And then Dickens gives us the reversal — which I find almost unbearably generous as a piece of storytelling.
Bella figures out what Boffin has actually been doing — performing corruption as a kind of moral education for her benefit.
And her speech to him is one of those moments where I have to put the book down and just sit with it for a minute.
She tells him — and she gives him a little shake as she says it —
"you showed her, in yourself, the most detestable sides of wealth, saying in your own mind,
'This shallow creature would never work the truth out of her own weak soul, if she had a hundred years to do it in;
but a glaring instance kept before her may open even her eyes and set her thinking.'"
The word 'fingerpost' — which comes just before — is the one I keep returning to.
A fingerpost just points — it doesn't lecture, it doesn't condemn — it simply shows you which road you're on.
That's what Boffin has been doing all along — and it's an act of love so patient it defeats the novel's own irony.
Caroline has landed on something I think is genuinely important, and I want to resist those readers who find the whole Boffin stratagem too contrived to bear.
The contrivance, as they call it, is rather the point.
Boffin is not a psychologist — he is, as Dickens takes pains to remind us, ignorant and unpolished.
His method is crude, theatrical, almost farcical — and it works precisely because goodness doesn't need sophistication.
That aphorism — Evil dies with the doer, but Good, never — that is Dickens's explanation of how Boffin can absorb the performance of greed without being destroyed by it.
The Good in him is structurally indestructible — and Dickens insists on that as a matter of moral law, not sentiment.
I'll accept that as moral philosophy — with one qualification.
The novel insists on Boffin's individual goodness surviving intact — and I believe that, within the fiction.
But Dickens is simultaneously telling us that the institutions — the dustheap, the Parliament, the boards — are not redeemed by individual virtue.
That mountain of pretentious failure is still there at the end of the novel.
Boffin can be a fingerpost for Bella — he cannot be a fingerpost for Parliament.
That is the tension at the centre of this novel that I don't think any reading fully resolves — and I suspect Dickens knew it.
And perhaps that irresolution is part of what makes the novel continue to live — a book that reaches a satisfying human ending while leaving the larger machinery running.
We'll be exploring more of that machinery — the legal, the social, the romantic — in the segments ahead.
Thank you to Sir Edmund, Professor Blackstone, and Caroline Woodcourt for a first conversation that has already produced more to think about than I can hold at once.

segments.title: The Doctrine of Exchange: What Dickens Believed About Goodness

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the programme that takes Dickens's last completed novel seriously — and slowly.
I'm joined today by three guests who bring very different lenses to this extraordinary book.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose belief that great fiction is first and last a moral art has never wavered.
Professor James Blackstone brings the historian's eye — he wants to know what the institutions actually were, and what they cost real people.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a critic who has read this novel many times and still stops to re-read sentences.
Today's question is one that runs under every page of Our Mutual Friend: what did Dickens actually believe about how goodness is made?
Is character fixed, or can it be taught — and if it can be taught, who does the teaching, and at what cost?
Edmund, let's begin with you — Bella Wilfer's transformation is perhaps the novel's most elaborately constructed moral argument.
Bella Wilfer is, I think, the figure through whom Dickens most honestly tests the question of whether character can be genuinely remade.
And what strikes me with particular force is a moment when she does not merely claim transformation — she demands to be tested by it.
She says to John Rokesmith — and the phrasing is quite precise:
That is not the language of sentiment — that is the language of moral seriousness.
She understands that happiness unearned, untested, is worth precisely nothing.
Dickens is quite Johnsonian here, actually — Johnson always insisted that virtue without trial is merely potential.
What moves me about that moment is not only the argument — it's the rhythm.
Try me through some reverse. Try me through some trial.
That repetition with variation — Dickens is imitating the very act of insistence, of self-conviction, in the sentence structure itself.
And she says she is not half, not a quarter, as worthy as she hopes to become.
That arithmetic of self-worth is quite heartbreaking — because she knows exactly how far she still has to go.
It's one of those Dickens moments where sentiment and precision are absolutely inseparable.
I want to come at this from a slightly different angle, if I may.
Edmund locates the moral argument in Bella — and that's right — but we should also ask who constructed the conditions for her transformation.
Bella herself, once the full scheme is revealed to her, articulates Mr Boffin's method with remarkable clarity.
That is a remarkably cold-eyed assessment of what pedagogical theatre actually requires.
Boffin decided that abstract moral instruction was useless — only a performed, embodied demonstration of corruption would work.
As a historian of institutions, I find that almost subversive: the philanthropist who teaches by pretending to be the very thing he despises.
James is quite right to press on Boffin's method — though I confess it troubles me theologically, if I may use the word loosely.
There is something almost Jesuit about it — the deliberate staging of evil in the service of good.
Burke would have found it deeply presumptuous — one man appointing himself the architect of another's soul.
And yet — Dickens does not let us doubt that Boffin's gamble succeeds.
Which tells us something rather uncomfortable about what Dickens believed: that goodness, left entirely to its own devices, may simply not arrive.
What I keep returning to is how extraordinary it is that Bella herself voices Boffin's design — that she works out his logic aloud and puts it to him directly.
She doesn't receive the explanation passively — she constructs it, tests it, offers it back.
That detail matters enormously because it means her transformation is not something done to her — she becomes its own interpreter.
And there's something very moving in the phrase
She is accusing herself with Boffin's eyes — which means she has genuinely inhabited the lesson.
Caroline's point about agency is important — but I'd push it further.
The novel insists that Bella's corruption was never really hers alone — it was produced by a specific environment of money, expectation, and frustrated inheritance.
What Boffin does is essentially replicate that environment in controlled conditions, like an experiment — and then remove the stimulus.
That's not Jesuit theology — that's almost clinical psychology, a century before anyone had the vocabulary for it.
So Dickens gives us a novel in which goodness must be constructed, not merely inherited or chosen — and the mechanism involves deception, patience, and risk.
Edmund finds that Johnsonian, James finds it proto-scientific, and Caroline finds it — if I've read you right — primarily generous.
What all three of you agree on, I think, is that Dickens does not let anyone off easily — not Bella, not Boffin, not the reader.
In a moment, we'll turn to the novel's darker architecture — to money, dust, and what the river asks of the people thrown into it.

segments.title: Institutions and Fog: The World Our Mutual Friend Actually Inhabited

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the programme that takes Dickens's last completed novel apart and puts it back together again.
I'm joined today by three guests who each bring something quite different to the table.

Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don and lifelong student of the English literary tradition, who believes that the novel's genius lies in its moral imagination — in individual character tested by circumstance.

Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who can tell us exactly what the institutions Dickens describes actually were, and what it meant, in hard material terms, to be poor in Victorian England.

And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has read this novel many times and cares passionately about the experience of reading it — what is funny, what is devastating, and what makes you stop mid-sentence.
Today's segment is about the world the novel actually inhabits — the fog, the river, the schools, the workhouse, the law.
Dickens doesn't just set his story in London — he builds an entire moral atmosphere from its physical conditions.
Let's begin with that atmosphere — with the fog.
The fog chapter stops me every single time I read it.
Dickens does something quite extraordinary there — he makes the fog do two contradictory things at once.
It both conceals and reveals — it makes the city stranger and more itself simultaneously.
And he finds this extraordinary phrase for it.
"Inanimate London was a sooty spectre, divided in purpose between being visible and invisible, and so being wholly neither."
"Wholly neither" — that's the crux of it.
The city is caught in a kind of ontological limbo — and so, I think, are most of its inhabitants.
That's beautifully put, and I wouldn't quarrel with it — but I'd resist pressing the fog too hard into service as social allegory.
What strikes me is the sheer exuberance of the writing — Dickens is enjoying himself enormously here.
Notice how the description moves through colour like a painter's palette — grey at the edges, dark yellow at the boundary, brown deepening inward, and then at the heart of the city, rusty-black.
And then he gives us this magnificent grotesque — the dome of Saint Paul's seeming to die hard above the fog.
That is the work of a novelist drunk on language — not a pamphleteer with a thesis.
The novelist and the pamphleteer are not always so easily separated, Sir Edmund — at least not in this book.
That fog — the real fog, the coal-smoke and sulphur dioxide that choked London for decades — killed people.
Dickens is not merely painting an atmosphere — he is indicting a system of production that treated the city and its poor as refuse.
The downriver journey makes that quite explicit — the carriage rolling through Ratcliffe and Rotherhithe, through territory that feels like the city's open drain.
Dickens writes of how the
"accumulated scum of humanity seemed to be washed from higher grounds, like so much moral sewage, and to be pausing until its own weight forced it over the bank and sunk it in the river."
Now — that phrase is uncomfortable, and deliberately so.
Dickens is adopting the language of the governing class — who did speak of the poor as sewage — and turning it back on them as accusation.
That's exactly the thing that makes the prose so unsettling on first reading — you're not always sure whether Dickens is ventriloquising that prejudice or endorsing it.
And then you read further into the book and you understand — it's the indictment, not the verdict.
The people who actually live along that river — the Hexams, Betty Higden — are treated with extraordinary dignity when we meet them.
I concede that the downriver passage is something more than atmospheric painting — there's a controlled fury in it.
But I'd locate that fury in the moral imagination of one man confronting suffering — not in any systematic programme.
Burke would have recognised that impulse — the conservative tradition has always held that society owes its poorest members something more than indifference.
And it's that failure of the institutions — the ones actually charged with alleviating that suffering — that brings us to the other great subject of this segment.
The schools, the Poor Law, the workhouse — James, you've looked closely at what those actually were.
The school Dickens describes in the Hexam chapters is a ragged school — a real institution, attended by children who had no other access to education.
Some of these schools did genuine good — but the conditions were often precisely as Dickens depicts them.
Overcrowded, chaotic, morally incoherent — the curriculum was a jumble of improving tracts and misapplied scripture.
And Dickens finds the perfect word for it.
"An exceedingly and confoundingly perplexing jumble of a school, in fact, where black spirits and grey, red spirits and white, jumbled jumbled jumbled jumbled, jumbled every night."
That incantatory repetition of 'jumbled' — it's not decoration.
It performs the very confusion it describes — it enacts the grinding, senseless repetition inflicted on those children.
And then the Sunday school passage — which is almost unbearable, actually.
The 'conventional volunteer boy' who smooths the faces of sleeping infants — that grotesque little bureaucrat of cruelty.
Dickens calls him the 'executioner's assistant' — and then describes the whole scene as if it were a High Market for contagious disease.
The comedy is savage — and the savagery is what makes it land.
What I find most telling in that passage is not the physical brutality but the intellectual corruption — the pretence that these young people are innocent children.
Dickens writes of 'young women old in the vices of the commonest and worst life' being expected to venerate the little improving tales of Little Margery.
The condescension of the lady-visitors — who enforce this nonsense — is, I think, Dickens's primary target.
It is the comfortable classes congratulating themselves on their charity while learning absolutely nothing about the people they claim to assist.
And the moral lesson of those improving tracts is quite as damning as the violence.
Thomas Twopence resolves not to rob his benefactor — and is rewarded with supernatural wealth.
Dickens points out, with lethal dryness, that the benefactor himself 'came to no good.'
The system teaches virtue as a species of self-interest — you do good not because it is good but, as Dickens says, 'because you were to make a good thing of it.'
That is the same logic that governs the Poor Law — and it poisons everything it touches.
Which brings us to the Poor Law directly — and to some of the most explicitly polemical writing in the entire novel.
The Poor Law Amendment Act of 1834 is the institutional backdrop to everything Dickens writes about poverty in this novel.
Its principle was deterrence — relief was made so deliberately unpleasant that only the truly destitute would seek it.
The workhouse test — you must enter the workhouse to receive any help — was designed to humiliate.
And Dickens understood exactly what this produced — a system so degrading that the most self-respecting of the poor would rather die than submit to it.
He states it with almost scriptural authority — listen to this passage.

"When we have got things to the pass that with an enormous treasure at disposal to relieve the poor, the best of the poor detest our mercies, hide their heads from us, and shame us by starving to death in the midst of us, it is a pass impossible of prosperity, impossible of continuance."
'The best of the poor' — that phrase does a great deal of work.
He is insisting that the system punishes virtue — that the prouder and more self-sufficient a person is, the more cruelly the Poor Law strikes them.
And here is where I find myself — perhaps surprisingly — in considerable agreement with Dickens.
The conservative tradition has never been indifferent to the claims of the poor — quite the reverse.
What it objects to is the utilitarian abstraction that reduces human beings to economic units — which is precisely what the Poor Law Amendment Act represented.
The wickedness of that system, as Dickens sees it, is that it is impersonal — it cannot distinguish the deserving from the undeserving because it does not look at persons at all.
Betty Higden is the embodiment of that argument — she walks herself to death across the English countryside rather than fall into the hands of the workhouse.
And what makes her so powerful as a character is that her fear is not irrational — it is the entirely reasonable response of a dignified person to an institution designed to strip her of dignity.
Dickens knew the critics would come for him on this — and he prepared his defence with remarkable precision.
He addresses those critics directly in the novel itself — which is an unusual thing to do, and speaks to how charged the debate was.
He dismisses the straw men — the people who accused him of wanting to give 'turtle soup and venison out of gold spoons' to every pauper.
And then he delivers his verdict on the Poor Law — and it is as unsparing as anything in English prose.
"I believe there has been in England, since the days of the Stuarts, no law so often infamously administered, no law so often openly violated, no law habitually so ill-supervised."
And then — because he will not let the illegality and the inhumanity be separated — he adds:

"In the majority of the shameful cases of disease and death from destitution, that shock the Public and disgrace the country, the illegality is quite equal to the inhumanity — and known language could say no more of their lawlessness."
'Known language could say no more' — he is claiming that he has reached the absolute limit of what words can do.
And yet the sentence itself is perfectly controlled — the fury is entirely contained within the form.
The rhetorical structure of that passage is remarkable — 'no law... no law... no law...' — the triple anaphora of a sermon.
He opens the chapter with 'my lords and gentlemen and honourable boards' — addressing Parliament itself.
And he closes with a prophecy — or a threat — that the system 'will mar every one of us' if left unreformed.
Whatever one thinks of his politics, that is the language of a man who believes with his whole being that literature has a duty — not merely a right — to speak.
That sense of duty — the novelist as witness, as accuser, as prophet — is a thread that runs through everything we've discussed today.
The fog, the river, the school, the Poor Law — they are not backdrop but argument.
The world of Our Mutual Friend is not simply the setting of a story — it is the story's central character.
My thanks to Sir Edmund Leigh, Professor James Blackstone, and Ms. Caroline Woodcourt.
We'll be back shortly with our next segment.

segments.title: Closing: Love, Self-Knowledge, and the Novel's Refusal to Despair

utterances.text: We've spent this episode moving through the darkest corners of Our Mutual Friend — the river, the dust heaps, the mercenary heart of London.
But Dickens, as ever, refuses to leave us there.
The novel's closing movement is about love and self-knowledge — and the strange, stubborn insistence that people can become better.
Edmund, I want to start with John Harmon — because his confession about why he came back to England is one of the most psychologically precise passages in the whole novel.
It is, and I think it is often undervalued precisely because it lacks theatrical decoration.
John Harmon is conducting a cross-examination of himself — and the verdict is unflinching.
The passage has this quality of a man who does not permit himself evasion.
He stops himself, and says — and this is the voice of genuine moral seriousness —
'Now, stop, and so far think it out, John Harmon. Is that so? That is exactly so.'
That little internal dialogue — question, answer — is a model of honest self-reckoning that Johnson himself would have approved.
And what Harmon is reckoning with is not merely a legal inheritance — it is the moral weight of his father's values, which he fears he has already begun to absorb.
What strikes me about that confession is the list — the sheer accumulation of mistrusts.
He is mistrustful of his father's intention, mistrustful of the prospective wife, mistrustful of himself.
And legally speaking, that suspicion was entirely rational.
Fortunes in this period were routinely used to bind marriages — to ensure property stayed within prescribed circles.
Harmon's father has done exactly that from beyond the grave.
The man has been dead for chapters, and he is still arranging people's lives.
What redeems Harmon is that he knows this — and chooses to test the inheritance of character, not just the inheritance of coin.
And that test falls on Bella — which brings me to the passage I find almost unbearably moving.
It is the Cherub — Bella's father — blessing the engagement.
He has built up to it with this slightly absurd running phrase — 'the mercenary young person distantly related to myself' — and then he lands the whole thing at once.
'My blessing on this engagement betwixt you, and she brings you a good fortune when she brings you the poverty she has accepted for your sake and the honest truth's!'
The poverty she has accepted for your sake and the honest truth's — that is a sentence I have read twenty times and it still catches me.
The Cherub has reframed the entire economy of the novel.
The verbal repetition there is doing something quite precise.
'The mercenary young person distantly related to myself' is repeated with such affectionate irony that by the third iteration the word mercenary has been entirely emptied of its charge.
It is a form of absolution through language.

Dickens understands — and I think this is one of the things that makes him great rather than merely popular — that a person can only be freed from a label by having it said aloud enough times to become ridiculous.
And it is the father giving that absolution — not a magistrate, not a benefactor.
The Cherub has almost no legal authority, no property, no standing in the world as the novel constructs it.
And yet his blessing carries more moral weight than any of the novel's wills and codicils.
That is a fairly pointed comment on where true authority resides.
Which brings us to the passage I find the most quietly devastating in the whole closing sequence.
Bella, at the end, cannot understand how she was loved.
She says — covering her face, which is the right gesture —

'It is, how John could love me so when I so little deserved it, and how you, Mr and Mrs Boffin, could be so forgetful of yourselves, and take such pains and trouble, to make me a little better, and after all to help him to so unworthy a wife.'
A little better — not transformed, not perfected.
Just a little better.
That is the most honest thing the novel says about what love and community can actually do.
And Bella does not say it with self-pity — she says it with gratitude.
The last words of her speech are 'I am very very grateful.'
Gratitude — proper gratitude, not performance — is, I would argue, the rarest and most demanding of the moral virtues.
Burke would have recognised it as the foundation of all social bonds.
Dickens arrives at the same place by a quite different road — through comedy, melodrama, and the river Thames.
I think what the novel refuses is despair — but not complacency.
The Veneerings are still at their table as the curtain falls.
The dust heaps have not gone anywhere.
But Bella can cover her face and say she is unworthy, and mean it with full sincerity, and that sincerity is the answer.
Not a structural solution — a human one.
That feels like the right note on which to close.
Our Mutual Friend is a novel that earns its happiness — through darkness, through self-examination, through the kind of love that makes itself worthy of its object.
My thanks to Sir Edmund Leigh, Professor James Blackstone, and Caroline Woodcourt for a conversation that has done justice to one of the great novels of the English language.
Thank you for listening to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.

c31:p1.text:
He went over it all again. He had lapsed into the condition in which he
      found himself, as many a man lapses into many a condition, without
      perceiving the accumulative power of its separate circumstances. When in
      the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil—never
      yet for good within his knowledge then—of his father and his
      father’s wealth on all within their influence, he conceived the idea of
      his first deception, it was meant to be harmless, it was to last but a few
      hours or days, it was to involve in it only the girl so capriciously
      forced upon him and upon whom he was so capriciously forced, and it was
      honestly meant well towards her. For, if he had found her unhappy in the
      prospect of that marriage (through her heart inclining to another man or
      for any other cause), he would seriously have said: ‘This is another of
      the old perverted uses of the misery-making money. I will let it go to my
      and my sister’s only protectors and friends.’ When the snare into which he
      fell so outstripped his first intention as that he found himself placarded
      by the police authorities upon the London walls for dead, he confusedly
      accepted the aid that fell upon him, without considering how firmly it
      must seem to fix the Boffins in their accession to the fortune. When he
      saw them, and knew them, and even from his vantage-ground of inspection
      could find no flaw in them, he asked himself, ‘And shall I come to life to
      dispossess such people as these?’ There was no good to set against the
      putting of them to that hard proof. He had heard from Bella’s own lips
      when he stood tapping at the door on that night of his taking the
      lodgings, that the marriage would have been on her part thoroughly
      mercenary. He had since tried her, in his own unknown person and supposed
      station, and she not only rejected his advances but resented them. Was it
      for him to have the shame of buying her, or the meanness of punishing her?
      Yet, by coming to life and accepting the condition of the inheritance, he
      must do the former; and by coming to life and rejecting it, he must do the
      latter.

When I devised this story, I foresaw the likelihood that a class of
      readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to
      conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John
      Harmon was not slain, and that Mr John Rokesmith was he. Pleasing myself

      ingenuity in the story, and thinking it worth while, in the interests of

      inconsistent little Beast?’
c38:p55.summary: Alone in her room, Bella grapples with her confused reaction to Mr Boffin's advice: she finds his sentiments sensible and true to her own desires, yet she is repelled by them and finds herself disparaging him for expressing them, finally questioning herself severely in the mirror.
c38:p55.best_quote: Why, what need to excuse him? What he said was very sensible, I am sure, and very true, I am sure. It is only what I often say to myself. Don't I like it then? No, I don't like it, and, though he is my liberal benefactor, I disparage him for it. Then pray, what do you mean by this, you inconsistent little Beast?

c38:p56.text:
The looking-glass preserving a discreet ministerial silence when thus
      called upon for explanation, Bella went to bed with a weariness upon her
      spirit which was more than the weariness of want of sleep. And again in
      the morning, she looked for the cloud, and for the deepening of the cloud,
      upon the Golden Dustman’s face.
c38:p56.summary: Bella goes to bed with a profound spiritual weariness, and the next morning she continues to observe the deepening cloud of corruption in the Golden Dustman's face.
c38:p56.best_quote: A weariness upon her spirit which was more than the weariness of want of sleep.

c42:p156.text:
The question was so directly at variance with Bella’s views in life, as
      set forth to her father, that she said internally, ‘There, you little
      mercenary wretch! Do you hear that? Ain’t you ashamed of your self?’ and
      unclasped the girdle of her arms, expressly to give herself a penitential
      poke in the side.
c42:p156.summary: Bella experiences an internal moment of shame at her own mercenary values when confronted by Lizzie's selfless love, and literally punishes herself with a poke in the side.
c42:p156.best_quote: There, you little mercenary wretch! Do you hear that? Ain't you ashamed of your self?

c42:p161.text:
Bella sat enchained by the deep, unselfish passion of this girl or woman
      of her own age, courageously revealing itself in the confidence of her
      sympathetic perception of its truth. And yet she had never experienced
      anything like it, or thought of the existence of anything like it.
c42:p161.summary: Bella is deeply moved by Lizzie's passionate confession of unselfish love, which represents something entirely new to her experience.

c49:p72.text:
‘Upon which,’ pursued the cherub, ‘the certain mercenary young person
      distantly related to myself, having previously observed and mentioned to
      myself that prosperity was spoiling Mr Boffin, felt that she must not sell
      her sense of what was right and what was wrong, and what was true and what
      was false, and what was just and what was unjust, for any price that could

c49:p72.summary: R. Wilfer describes how Bella, seeing Mr Boffin corrupted by wealth, resolved not to sell her moral principles for any price.
c49:p72.best_quote: this mercenary young person distantly related to myself, having previously observed and mentioned to myself that prosperity was spoiling Mr Boffin, felt that she must not sell her sense of what was right and what was wrong, and what was true and what was false, and what was just and what was unjust, for any price that could be paid to her by any one alive?

c16:p31.text:
‘For I aint, you must know,’ said Betty, ‘much of a hand at reading
      writing-hand, though I can read my Bible and most print. And I do love a
      newspaper. You mightn’t think it, but Sloppy is a beautiful reader of a

c2:p52.text:
‘And a ladder and basket if you like. By which means, or by others, he
      grew rich as a Dust Contractor, and lived in a hollow in a hilly country
      entirely composed of Dust. On his own small estate the growling old
      vagabond threw up his own mountain range, like an old volcano, and its
